{{Short description|Terminology leading to erroneous conclusions}}
'''Jingle-jangle fallacies''' are erroneous assumptions that either two different things are the same because they bear the same name (''jingle'' fallacy); or two identical or almost identical things are different because they are labeled differently (''jangle'' fallacy).<ref>{{cite book |last1= Kelley |first1= Truman Lee |title= Interpretation of Educational Measurements |year= 1927 |publisher= World Book Company |location= Yonkers-on-Hudson, N.Y. |pages= 62–65 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1= Roeser |first1= Robert W. |last2= Peck |first2= Stephen C. |last3= Nasir |first3= Nailah Suad |editor1-first= Patricia k. |editor1-last= Alexander |editor2-first= Philip H. |editor2-last= Winne |title= Handbook of Educational Psychology |url= https://archive.org/details/handbookofeducat0002unse/page/392 |edition= 2nd |year= 2006 |publisher= Erlbaum |location= Mahwah, N.J. |isbn= 978-0-8058-4937-0 |pages= [https://archive.org/details/handbookofeducat0002unse/page/392 392–393] |chapter= Self and Identity Processes in School Motivation, Learning, and Achievement |chapter-url= https://books.google.com/books?id=iSixyjjdq4gC&pg=PA393 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1= Pedhazur |first1= Elazar J. |last2= Pedhazur Schmelkin |first2= Liora |title= Measurement, Design, and Analysis: An Integrated Approach |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=2Y1RXHYO9UUC&pg=PA74 |year= 1991 |publisher= Erlbaum |location= Hillsdale, N.J. |isbn= 978-0-89859-555-0 |page= 74 }}</ref> The term was coined by [[Truman Lee Kelley]] in his 1927 book ''Interpretation of educational measurements''.<ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Zd0jAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA64 | title=Interpretation of Educational Measurements | isbn=978-0-598-43399-2 | last1=Kelley | first1=Truman Lee | date=1927 | publisher=World Book Company }}</ref> In research, a jangle fallacy is the inference that two measures (e.g., tests, scales) with different names measure different [[Construct (philosophy of science)|constructs]]. By comparison, a jingle fallacy is the assumption that two measures which are called by the same name capture the same construct.<ref>{{cite book |last1= Corsini |first1= Raymond J. |title= The Dictionary of Psychology |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=0uxnglHzYaoC&pg=PA513 |year= 1991 |publisher= Routledge |location= New York |isbn= 978-1-58391-328-4 |pages= 513, 514 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1= Marsh |first1= Herbert W. |editor1-first= Sophia |editor1-last= Jowett |editor2-first= David |editor2-last= Lavallee |title= Social Psychology in Sport |year= 2007 |publisher= Human Kinetics |location= Champaign, IL |isbn= 978-0-7360-5780-6 |page= 168 |chapter= Physical Self-Concept and Sport |chapter-url= https://books.google.com/books?id=t6sx0cj3GUoC&pg=PA168 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1= Thorndike |first1= Edward |title= An Introduction to the Theory of Mental and Social Measures |year= 1904 |publisher= Teachers College, Columbia University |location= New York, NY |pages= 10–11 }}</ref>

==Examples==
An example of the jangle fallacy can be found in tests designed to assess [[emotional intelligence]]. Some of these tests merely measure personality or regular [[Intelligence quotient|IQ]].<ref>{{cite book |last1= Gignac |first1= Gilles E. |editor1-first= Con |editor1-last= Stough |editor2-first= Donald H. |editor2-last= Saklofske |editor3-first= James D. A.|editor3-last= Parker |title= Assessing Emotional Intelligence: Theory, Research, and Applications |year= 2009 |publisher= Springer |location= New York |isbn= 978-0-387-88370-0 |page= 33 |chapter= Psychometrics and the Measurement of Emotional Intelligence |chapter-url= https://books.google.com/books?id=LHsoQUXiV5AC&pg=PA33 }}</ref> An example of the jingle fallacy is that personality and values are sometimes conflated and treated as the same construct.<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Higgs |first1= Malcolm |last2= Scott |first2= Lichtenstein | year= 2010 | title= Exploring the 'Jingle Fallacy': a study of personality and values |journal= Journal of General Management |volume= 36 |issue= 1| pages= 43&ndash;61|doi= 10.1177/030630701003600103 }}</ref> Jingle and jangle fallacies make it challenging to review literatures for [[meta-analysis]].  Machine learning tools have been created to discover relevant papers even when the same construct is named differently in different articles.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Larsen |first1=Kai R. |last2=Bong |first2=Chih How |date=2016-03-03 |title=A Tool for Addressing Construct Identity in Literature Reviews and Meta-Analyses |url=https://misq.org/a-tool-for-addressing-construct-identity-in-literature-reviews-and-meta-analyses.html |journal=MIS Quarterly |volume=40 |issue=3 |pages=529–551 |doi=10.25300/MISQ/2016/40.3.01}}</ref> Some authors have stated that the personality traits [[Machiavellianism scale|Machiavellianism]] and [[psychopathy]] represent the issue of a jangle fallacy, as both constructs are named differently yet describe the same concept.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://doi=10.1007/s12144-019-00518-0 | doi=10.1007/s12144-019-00518-0 | title=The Dark Triad and facets of personality | date=2021 | last1=Kowalski | first1=Christopher Marcin | last2=Vernon | first2=Philip A. | last3=Schermer | first3=Julie Aitken | journal=Current Psychology | volume=40 | issue=11 | pages=5547–5558 }}</ref> A recent paper published in 2022 stated that Machiavellianism "is theoretically distinct from psychopathy, but empirically they are nearly indistinguishable".<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://doi=10.1111/spc3.12662 | doi=10.1111/spc3.12662 | title=Taking an elemental approach to the conceptualization and measurement of Machiavellianism, narcissism, and psychopathy | date=2022 | last1=Kay | first1=Cameron S. | last2=Arrow | first2=Holly | journal=Social and Personality Psychology Compass | volume=16 | issue=4 }}</ref>

==Views on the phenomenon==

Herbert Marsh highlighted the issue of jingle-jangle fallacies through a [[factor analysis]] of two distinct motivation assessments.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://doi.org/10.1123/jsep.16.4.365 | doi=10.1123/jsep.16.4.365 | title=Sport Motivation Orientations: Beware of Jingle-Jangle Fallacies | date=1994 | last1=Marsh | first1=Herbert W. | journal=Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology | volume=16 | issue=4 | pages=365–380 }}</ref><ref name="Marsh">Marsh, Herbert W., Reinhard Pekrun, Philip D. Parker, Kou Murayama, Jiesi Guo, Theresa Dicke, and A. Katrin Arens. "The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies." Journal of educational psychology 111, no. 2 (2019): 331.</ref> His analysis revealed that while the mastery and performance subscales from both instruments aligned with shared underlying factors, the competition subscales, despite being labeled identically, actually represented different psychological constructs: one tied to performance orientation, the other to task orientation.<ref name="Marsh"/> This discrepancy illustrates the importance of conducting thorough construct validity studies to evaluate the true meaning behind measurement instruments. Simply demonstrating that items from a single scale load onto one factor when assessed in isolation does not confirm their distinctiveness when compared with items from other constructs in a broader factor analysis. Moreover, assigning a label to a factor does not justify assumptions about its relationship to other constructs, regardless of how similar or different they might appear.<ref name="Marsh"/> Heyman and Dweck (1992) also warned that researchers must ensure they are not inadvertently measuring the same construct under different names.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00991653 | doi=10.1007/BF00991653 | title=Achievement goals and intrinsic motivation: Their relation and their role in adaptive motivation | date=1992 | last1=Heyman | first1=Gail D. | last2=Dweck | first2=Carol S. | journal=Motivation and Emotion | volume=16 | issue=3 | pages=231–247 }}</ref> Pajares (2009) echoed this concern, pointing out how conceptually similar variables may be operationalized differently across studies to serve specific research aims, often leading to confusion, particularly when perceptions of competence are misrepresented as [[self-efficacy]].<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://doi.org/10.1080/00220670109598780 | doi=10.1080/00220670109598780 | title=Toward a Positive Psychology of Academic Motivation | date=2001 | last1=Pajares | first1=Frank | journal=The Journal of Educational Research | volume=95 | pages=27–35 }}</ref> Likewise, Bong & Skaalvik (2003) recommended the use of [[confirmatory factor analysis]] (CFA) and structural equation modeling (SEM) to rigorously test the structural, predictive, convergent, and discriminant validity of motivational constructs, helping to avoid what they termed a "conceptual mess."<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1021302408382 | doi=10.1023/A:1021302408382 | date=2003 | last1=Bong | first1=Mimi | last2=Skaalvik | first2=Einar M. | title=Academic Self-Concept and Self-Efficacy: How Different Are They Really? | journal=Educational Psychology Review | volume=15 | issue=1 | pages=1–40 }}</ref>
